1.title: The Red Hen
1.topic: hen finds a rock in the yard
1.text: Jen has a red hen. The hen digs in the yard. She digs in the mud all day. One day the hen digs up a rock. The rock is flat and wet. Jen picks it up. The sun hits the rock. It shines! Jen runs to show her mom. Mom looks at it and smiles. What a grand rock! Jen sets the rock on a shelf. The hen steps in the yard. Jen gives the hen a pat. Good job, red hen! Now Jen digs with the hen. They dig and dig. What will they find next?

1.title: Rex at the Park
1.topic: dog digs up lost balls at the park
1.text: Ben and his dog Rex go to the park. Ben has a ball. He tosses it far. Rex runs fast to get it. Then Rex stops at a big bush. He digs and digs. Ben runs to look. Rex has found a ball in the mud! He digs up two more. Three lost balls! The balls are old but still good. Ben picks them up. Other kids lost these balls, he thinks. Ben sets the balls on the bench. Now the kids can find them. Rex wags and wags. Ben grins at him. Good dog, Rex!

1.title: The Box Fort
1.topic: cat and kids build a box fort
1.text: A big box sat on the rug. Sam got in the box. His cat, Max, got in too. Sam cut a flap in the side. Now the box has a door! Max naps on Sam's lap. Then Sam gets a red pen. He adds dots and stars to the box. His sis, Meg, brings one more box. They set the two together. Now it is a fort! Sam is in one box. Meg is in the next box. Max sits on top of it all. The fort is the best spot to be.

1.title: Mud Buns
1.topic: making mud buns in the sun
1.text: Deb and Tom mix mud in a big tin pan. They add a bit of grass on top. Then they roll the mud into buns. Six fat mud buns! They set the pan in the hot sun. The sun bakes the buns all day. At last the buns get hard. Deb taps one with a stick. Tap, tap! It is as hard as a rock. Tom adds one small twig on top of each bun. Now they look grand. They do not munch them! It is just for fun. Mud buns are the best kind of mess.

1.title: On the Bus
1.topic: the ride to school on the bus
1.text: The big bus stops at the end of my block. I get on and sit with my pal, Kim. The bus hums and off we go. I look out at the shops. I see a man with ten dogs! Kim sees a red truck. Next we pass a park with swings. The bus stops six more times. More kids get on. They chat and grin. At last I can see the school. The bus pulls in and stops. We hop off. In we go! The bus trip is fun. I like the bus.

1.title: Frogs on the Log
1.text: Nat and Gus go to the pond. A big log sits in the wet mud. One frog hops on the log. Then two more frogs hop up. Now three frogs sit on the log! A duck swims past them. Plop! One frog hops off. Gus grins. Two frogs are left, he says. A bug zips past the log. Snap! A frog gets it. Nat claps. The sun gets low. The frogs hop off the log. Plip, plop, plip! The pond is still. Nat and Gus go up the path. What a fun trip to the pond!

1.title: The Lost Sock
1.topic: hunting for a lost sock on wash day
1.text: It is wash day at my house. I help Mom sort the socks. Red socks, tan socks, big socks, small socks. But one black sock has no match! I check the rug. No sock. I check my bed. No sock. I check the wash bin. Not there. Then I spot the dog in his bed. A black tip sticks out! It is the lost sock. Bad pup! He just grins at me. I get the sock and set it with its match. Mom gives me a wink. Wash day ends well. Each sock has its pal.

1.title: The Bug in the Grass
1.topic: watching a bug and drawing it
1.text: Deb sits in the grass with her pad and pen. A small red bug lands on her hand. It has six legs and black dots. The bug does not nip. It just sits. Deb holds still. The bug walks up her hand. It stops at her cuff. Then it lifts its shell. Zip! It is off! Deb gets her pen. She adds the bug to her pad. Red back, black dots, six legs. She adds the sun and the grass as well. Mom pins the pad up. Best bug pic yet! Deb will hunt for more bugs at dusk.

1.title: The Lunch Box
1.topic: packing a lunch box with dad
1.text: Dad and I pack my lunch box. We put in a ham bun. Next, a red plum. Then six crisp chips in a small bag. Dad adds a can of milk. I tuck in a snack for my pal Sid. It is a big fig bar. Sid asks for figs a lot! I zip the box shut. Snap! The lid clicks. My lunch box is fat and full. When the bell rings, I will sit with Sid. We will munch and chat. The best bit? The fig bar. Yum!

1.title: The Wind and the Hat
1.topic: chasing a hat on a windy day
1.text: The wind is big and fast. It flaps the flags on the shops. Dad and I walk to the park. Zip! The wind grabs Dad's hat. The hat flips and spins. We run and run. The hat lands on a bench. Dad grabs at it. Zip! Off it flips. A big kid stops it. He picks it up. He hands the hat to Dad. Dad grins and nods. The kid grins back. Dad jams the hat back on. He holds it as we walk. The wind still huffs and puffs. But now the hat is snug. The wind will not get it!

2.title: A Snail for the Tank
2.topic: classroom fish tank gets a snail
2.text: Our class has a fish tank by the window. Five little fish swim in it all day. Last week our teacher brought in a small snail. The snail rides on the glass wall of the tank. It slides along on one flat foot. We watch it clean the glass as it goes. The fish did not seem to mind the new pet. Each morning we check on the snail first. It naps under a green leaf when the room is loud. We made a chart to track how far it slides each day. So far its best trip is the whole side of the tank! A snail is slow, but it always gets there. Our tank is a better home with the snail in it.

2.title: Kite Day
2.topic: flying a kite on a windy hill
2.text: Jack and his gram made a kite from a paper bag. They gave it a long tail made of rags. Then they went up the green hill to fly it. The wind on the hill was just right. Gram held the kite up high. Jack ran with the string and the kite rose! It went up and up over the trees. The tail waved like a happy flag. When the wind got soft, the kite began to dip. Jack tugged the string and it rose again. He found out that a kite needs wind pushing on it to stay up. They flew the kite until the sun got low. Then they rolled up the string and went home. Best day yet, said Jack.

2.title: The Lost Mitten
2.topic: a lost mitten travels along the street
2.text: A small blue mitten sat on the snowy path. A baker saw it first and picked it up. He set it on a post so it could be seen. A girl with a sled saw it next. She put it up on the gate by the shop. Then a mail man spotted it there. He clipped it to the rail with a pin and a note. The note said, is this your mitten? At last a boy named Finn came down the path. One of his hands was cold and bare! He saw the blue mitten on the rail and cheered. He slid it on and waved his warm hand. Three helpers had passed his mitten along. A whole street helped one cold hand find its mitten.

2.title: Beans in a Cup
2.topic: planting bean seeds and tracking sprouts
2.text: On Monday we planted bean seeds in clear cups. We set wet paper in each cup so we could see the seeds grow. My seed sat still for three long days. I checked it each morning and wrote a note. On day four a tiny white root poked out! It grew down, not up. That is how roots always grow. On day six a green stem curled up out of the seed. It found the light at the window. By day ten my bean had two flat leaves. The root had little hairs all over it. My chart shows the plant grew one inch in one week. Next we will move the beans to real dirt outside. I cannot wait to see how tall mine gets.

2.title: My Library Card
2.text: Today I got my very own library card. I printed my name on a line and the helper typed it in. She handed me a card with a bird on it. This card lets you take home ten books, she said. Ten books! I went straight to the shelves. I picked a book about big cats and one about the moon. I picked a funny one about a duck who bakes. At the desk I set my card on the scanner. It beeped one time for each book. The helper slid the books to me in a neat stack. Mine, all mine, for three whole weeks! I hugged the stack all the way home. I will read one each night. Then I will go back for more.

2.title: Two Shadows
2.topic: tracing shadows at two times of day
2.text: On a sunny morning we went out with chalk. I stood on the playground and Meg traced my shadow. It was long and thin. It stretched way past the swings. We wrote the time next to it. At noon we went back to the same spot. I stood on the same marks. But my shadow had moved! Now it was short and fat. It hid right under me. Meg traced it again with red chalk. Two shadows, one kid! Our teacher asked, what moved? Not you, she said. The sun did. When the sun is low, shadows are long. When the sun is high, shadows are small. We will trace one more shadow before we go home. I think it will be long again. Shadow chalk is the best kind of math.

2.title: Butter in a Jar
2.text: Our class made butter today, and all we used was cream and a jar. Our teacher poured the cream in and shut the lid tight. Then we took turns shaking the jar. Shake, shake, shake! At first it just sloshed. My arms got tired fast, so I passed the jar to Ben. After a while the sloshing stopped. We heard a soft thump inside. We opened the lid and peeked in. A yellow lump sat in thin milk! The lump was butter. The thin milk around it even has a name. It is called buttermilk. We rinsed the lump and added a tiny bit of salt. Then we spread it on crackers. Fresh crackers and fresh butter! Making food is fun, but making it with your own hands is even better.

2.title: Where Did the Puddle Go?
2.topic: a puddle shrinks after the rain
2.text: After the rain stopped, a big puddle sat on our steps. It was as wide as a bike wheel. Jen drew a chalk line all around it. Then we went in for lunch. When we came back, the puddle was smaller! It had shrunk away from the chalk line. Jen drew a new line. We checked again before dinner. Smaller still! By the next morning the puddle was gone. But where did it go? It did not run off. The steps are flat. Our teacher says the sun turns water into a mist too fine to see. The water rises into the air bit by bit. That is called drying up, and the chalk rings proved it happened. Four rings, one gone puddle. Now when I see a puddle, I know the sun is drinking it.

2.title: Sorting Day
2.text: On Friday our class runs the sorting station. Three big bins wait by the door. One bin is for cans. One is for glass jars. One is for clean paper. Kids from each room bring us their stuff. We check each thing before it drops in a bin. A can with food still inside gets rinsed first. A torn box gets pressed flat. Caps come off the jars. My job this week is the paper bin. I stack the sheets in a neat pile. Full bins get rolled out to the big truck on wheels. The driver waves at us each time. Our teacher keeps a chart of what we save. Last month it was nine full bins! Sorting is a small job. But small jobs add up week after week.

2.title: First Swim Class
2.topic: learning to float and kick at swim class
2.text: Last week I started swim class at the town pool. At first I held the wall and kicked my legs. Splash, splash! The teacher showed us how to blow bubbles in the water. You blow out when your face is in the water. You breathe in when your face is out. Then we each got a float board. I held mine tight and kicked across the shallow end. The water helped hold me up. Soon I could glide three whole feet with no kicks at all! My pal Finn can float on his back like a starfish. I am still learning that one. My legs sink each time. At the end of class we all jump in from the side. That is the best part. Next week we learn big arm circles. I can not wait to swim for real.

3.title: Follow That Ant
3.text: Have you ever seen a line of ants marching across a sidewalk? The ants are not just walking in a row for fun. They are following a smell. When an ant finds food, it walks home and leaves a trail of scent behind it. Other ants smell the trail and follow it straight to the food. Each ant that makes the trip adds more scent to the path. That makes the trail stronger, so even more ants can find it. When the food is gone, the ants stop adding scent. The old trail slowly fades away, and the ants stop coming. The path is not drawn on the ground. It is made of smell, and smells fade. You can test this with a leaf. Set it across the trail and the ants will scatter. They lost the scent! Soon they find the path again on the other side. A tiny ant cannot see very far, but its nose always knows the way.

3.title: The Marble Run
3.topic: building a marble run from tubes
3.text: Nora saved paper tubes for a month to build a marble run. She taped the first tube to the wall so it tilted down. The marble rolled through it and shot out the end. Next she added a second tube going the other way. Now the marble zigzagged down the wall. But there was a problem. The marble flew out between the tubes and rolled under the couch. Nora studied the gap. The marble was moving too fast to turn. She made the first tube less steep and taped a cup at the corner. This time the marble dropped into the cup, rolled out a hole she had cut, and slid into the next tube. It worked! By bedtime the run had seven tubes, two cups, and one small bell at the bottom. Every marble that made the full trip rang the bell. Nora had built her machine one fix at a time.

3.title: The Little Book Box
3.text: A new box stands at the corner of our street. It looks like a tiny house on a post, with a glass door and one shelf. It is full of books. A sign on it says, take a book, leave a book. Anyone may open the door and borrow whatever looks good. There is no card and no due date. The deal is simple. When you can, you leave a book of your own for the next reader. On Monday the box held ten books. By Friday it held ten different ones. The books keep moving from hand to hand around the neighborhood. A girl left a joke book and took one about sharks. An old man left two mysteries and took a book of maps. Nobody runs the box. The readers run it together, one trade at a time. It might be the smallest library in town, and the busiest shelf on the street.

3.title: Busy Builders
3.topic: how beavers build dams and lodges
3.text: A beaver is a builder that never went to school. Its front teeth are strong and sharp. It can cut down a small tree in one night. The beaver drags branches into a stream and piles them up. Then it packs mud into the gaps. This wall of sticks and mud is called a dam. The dam slows the stream. A deep, quiet pond spreads out behind it. That pond is exactly what the beaver wants. In the middle of the pond, the beaver builds its home, called a lodge. The only doors are underwater. The beaver swims in and out, and most other animals cannot follow it inside. Above the water line there is a dry room for sleeping. The pond helps other creatures too. Frogs, fish, and ducks all move into the calm water. One furry builder with big teeth can change a whole stream into a busy pond.

3.title: Skipping Stones
3.topic: learning to skip stones on a lake
3.text: My uncle can make a stone dance across a lake. The stone hops off the water four or five times before it sinks. He says any kid can learn it, and the trick has three parts. First, pick the right stone. It should be flat, smooth, and about as wide as a cookie. Round or lumpy stones sink right away. Second, hold it flat with one finger curled around the edge. Third, throw it sideways and low, so the stone spins as it leaves your hand. The spin keeps it steady, like a rolling wheel that will not tip over. When the flat bottom smacks the water at a low angle, the water pushes it back up for another hop. My first ten throws all sank with a plop. Then one stone skipped twice, and I cheered. By the end of the day I got four hops. My uncle just smiled and said, now try for five.

3.title: The Web Builder
3.topic: how a spider builds an orb web
3.text: A garden spider builds a new web almost every night, and she does it in the dark. First she lets out a long thread and waits. The breeze carries it across the gap until it sticks to a branch. That first thread is her bridge. She walks across it and drops a second line below, making a big Y shape. Next come the spokes. She adds thread after thread from the center out, like the spokes of a wheel. None of these threads are sticky. They are her walking paths. Then comes the trap. Starting at the outside, she lays a long spiral of sticky silk, row after row, all the way to the middle. Bugs that fly into it are stuck at once. The spider feels the web shake and runs out along a dry spoke. Her own feet stay safe on the paths she planned. By morning the web sparkles. By night it may be torn. That is fine with her. She eats the old silk and builds it all again.

3.title: Why Leaves Turn
3.topic: why leaves change color in fall
3.text: All summer long, a maple leaf is a little green machine. The green comes from a helper inside the leaf that catches sunlight and turns it into food for the tree. There is so much green helper in each leaf that no other color can show. But the green was never the only color there. Yellow and orange hide in the leaf all summer, under all that green. When fall comes, the days get short and cold is on the way. The tree gets ready to rest. It stops making the green helper, and the old green fades away. Now the yellow and orange can finally show! They were there the whole time. Some trees do even more. They make a brand new red color in the fall, and no one is fully sure why. Soon the tree lets its leaves drop. A bare tree loses less water in winter, and it will grow new leaves in spring. So fall colors are not really new paint. They are old colors coming out of hiding.

3.title: The Light That Talks
3.text: A lighthouse does more than shine. It talks. Every lighthouse flashes in its own pattern, and sailors know each pattern by heart. One light may flash twice, then rest. Another may flash every ten seconds. The pattern works like a name tag. A sailor who sees two quick flashes in the dark can check a chart and say, that is the light on the north point! Now the ship knows where it is. The light itself does not blink on and off. Inside the tower, a giant glass lens spins slowly around a bright lamp. The lens gathers the lamp's glow and squeezes it into strong beams. Each time a beam sweeps past a ship, the sailors see a flash. Long ago, a keeper lived at each lighthouse. The keeper wound the gears that spun the lens and kept the lamp burning all night. Today, machines do that work. But the lights still flash their names to the sea, all night, every night, just as they always have.

3.title: From Tree to Syrup
3.text: Real maple syrup starts as a clear liquid called sap, and it comes straight out of a tree. In late winter, sap moves up and down inside maple trees. Sugar makers drill a small hole in the trunk and tap in a little spout. Drip, drip, drip! The sap runs into a bucket or a tube. The drilling does not harm a healthy tree. A big maple has sap to spare. The best sap weather is odd. It takes cold nights and mild days. If it stays warm, the sap stops running. Fresh sap looks like water and barely tastes sweet. The magic happens in the sugar house. The sap boils in wide pans for hours, and steam rolls out the roof. As the water steams away, the sugar left behind gets thicker and darker. It takes about forty buckets of sap to make just one bucket of syrup! That is why real maple syrup costs more than the fake kind. Every golden drop began as a winter tree, one drip at a time.

3.title: The Bird That Finds Home
3.text: A homing pigeon can be driven far away and set free in a strange place. It will still fly straight home. Some birds have found their way back from hundreds of miles away. How do they do it? When a pigeon is set loose, it circles up into the sky a few times. It seems to be checking the land below and the sun above. Scientists think pigeons use several tricks at once. They watch the sun's spot in the sky like a clock. They follow rivers, roads, and hills they have seen before. Many scientists think pigeons can also feel which way is north. A compass needle feels that same pull. No single trick explains it all. That puzzle is part of why people love these birds. Long before phones, people put tiny rolled notes in little tubes on pigeons' legs. The birds carried news home faster than any rider on a horse. Today people race them for sport. The pigeons do not know they are racing. They just know one thing very well. Home is that way.

4.title: The Dance of the Bees
4.text: When a honeybee finds a patch of flowers full of nectar, she does not keep the news to herself. She flies back to the hive and tells the other bees exactly where the flowers are. Her message is not spoken or written. It is danced. On the wall of the hive, the bee runs forward in a straight line while waggling her body from side to side. Then she circles back and repeats the run, over and over. The other bees crowd around her in the dark and read the dance. The direction of her waggle run tells them which way to fly compared to the sun. The length of the run tells them how far to go. A short waggle means the flowers are close. A long one means a far trip. Scientists tested this by watching dancing bees and then following the fliers that had watched. The watchers flew almost straight to the flower patch, just as the dance had promised. A bee's brain is smaller than a grain of rice, yet it can send a map made of motion.

4.title: Why the Moon Changes Shape
4.text: The moon seems to change shape all month long. One week it is a thin sliver, and two weeks later it is a bright full circle. But the moon itself never changes shape at all. What changes is how much of its lit side we can see. The moon makes no light of its own. Sunlight always brightens the half of the moon that faces the sun. Think of a ball in sunshine. One side of the ball is bright, and the other side is in shade. The moon works the same way. As the moon travels around Earth, we see its lit half from different angles. When the moon sits between Earth and the sun, its bright side faces away from us. We see almost nothing then. When Earth sits between the sun and the moon, the whole lit side faces us, and we see a full moon. In between come the slivers, halves, and lopsided shapes on the calendar. The next time the moon looks broken or thin, remember that nothing is missing. You are simply seeing daylight on another world, one slice at a time.

4.title: The Compost Bin
4.topic: how a school compost bin turns scraps to soil
4.text: Behind our school cafeteria stands a wooden bin that eats lunch every day. Into it go apple cores, banana peels, carrot ends, and stale bread. This is the compost bin, and inside it, garbage slowly becomes rich, dark soil. The real workers are too small to see. Bacteria and molds break the scraps down, and as they work, the pile heats up. On a cold morning you can see steam rising from it. Worms and beetles move in and grind the softened scraps even finer. The pile needs air, so once a week a class turns it over with a garden fork. It needs water too, about as damp as a wrung-out sponge. Meat and cheese stay out because they attract rats. After a few months, the bottom of the pile does not look like food scraps anymore. It is crumbly and brown, and it smells like a forest floor. In spring we shovel it into the garden beds, where it feeds the new tomato plants. Last year's lunch, it turns out, grows this year's lunch. The bin never stops working, and neither do its tiny crew.

4.title: Bottles That Ride the Sea
4.text: More than a hundred years ago, scientists began tossing glass bottles into the sea on purpose. Each drift bottle held a numbered postcard. The card asked the finder to write down where the bottle washed up, and when. The bottles could not steer or paddle. They simply rode the water, and that made them perfect tools. Wherever a bottle went, the ocean itself had carried it. Slowly, the postcards came back in the mail. Thousands of cards piled up over the years. Then mapmakers connected the dots. Bottles dropped near one coast kept landing on the same faraway beaches, sometimes years later. The paths they traced showed the ocean's great rivers, called currents. These wide streams flow through the sea without any banks. One famous bottle drifted in a huge circle for many years. At last a beach walker picked it up. Today, scientists track the water with floating robots. The robots report by satellite many times a day. But the humble bottle proved the big idea first. If you want to know where water goes, give it something to carry. Then wait, and let the sea mail you the answer.

4.title: The Story of the Pencil
4.topic: history of the pencil and graphite
4.text: The pencil in your desk has no lead in it, even though people call it a lead pencil. The dark writing material is graphite, a soft and slippery form of carbon. Long ago in England, sheep farmers found a strange black rock. It lay under the roots of a fallen tree. The rock marked their hands. It also wrote a smoother line than any stick of charcoal. Soon everyone wanted the marking stone. But it broke easily, and it turned fingers black. Wrapping it in string helped only a little. The real fix came from woodworkers. They cut a groove into a thin strip of cedar, laid a rod of graphite inside, and glued a second strip on top. Now the graphite had a wooden jacket. Later, pencil makers learned an even better trick. They ground graphite into powder, mixed it with clay, and baked it hard. More clay made a harder, lighter line. Less clay made a softer, darker one. That recipe still sets the numbers printed on pencils today. A pencil seems simple. Yet it took farmers, woodworkers, and chemists working over many years to put one in your hand.

4.title: The Truth About Chameleons
4.text: Most people think a chameleon changes color to match whatever it sits on. Put it on red, it turns red. Put it on plaid, it panics. That is the story, but it is mostly wrong. A chameleon's color changes are not really about hiding. They are about talking. A calm chameleon usually wears dull green or brown, which already blends in with leaves and branches. The bright changes happen when the animal has something to say. A male who wants to warn off a rival flashes bold stripes and hot colors. A chameleon that feels cold turns darker, because dark skin soaks up more warmth from the sun. A relaxed one turns pale again. The skin itself works in an amazing way. Under the surface lie tiny crystals, stacked in neat rows. When the chameleon tightens or relaxes its skin, the spacing of the crystals changes, and the skin reflects different colors of light. It is less like painting and more like tuning. So a chameleon is not a master of disguise trying to copy your shirt. It is more like a walking mood ring, telling the world exactly how it feels.

4.title: A World in a Jar
4.topic: a sealed terrarium recycles its own water
4.text: You can grow a garden inside a closed glass jar, seal the lid, and never water it again. That sounds impossible, but it works, and some sealed jar gardens have stayed green for many years. The trick is that the jar recycles everything. Here is a day inside the jar. The plant's roots drink water from the damp soil. The water travels up the stem to the leaves. The leaves release some of it into the air as an invisible vapor. Soon the air in the jar is loaded with moisture. When the vapor touches the cool glass, it turns back into drops. The glass fogs up, and little beads of water slide down the walls, back into the soil. That is rain, indoors, on a garden the size of your hand. The same water goes around and around, day after day. Earth works much the same way. Water rises from oceans and lakes, forms clouds, falls again, and returns to the sea. Our planet is a sealed jar too, just a very large one. Nothing new is ever added. The water you drank today has been riding that loop for a very, very long time.

4.title: Why Popcorn Pops
4.topic: the science inside a popcorn kernel
4.text: A popcorn kernel is a tiny sealed container, and that is the whole secret. Inside the hard yellow shell sits a bit of soft starch and a drop of water. Most kinds of corn have shells that leak, but popcorn's shell is special. It is hard, smooth, and nearly airtight. When you heat the kernel, the drop of water inside gets hotter and hotter. It wants to boil away into steam, but the steam has nowhere to go. The sealed shell traps it. So the pressure inside the kernel builds, and builds, and builds. The soft starch melts into something like thick dough. Finally the shell cannot hold on any longer. It splits, and everything happens at once. The steam bursts free, the melted starch puffs out into a white foam, and the foam cools and sets in the blink of an eye. That white fluffy part you eat is puffed starch, frozen in mid-explosion. The pop you hear is the shell letting go. And those sad kernels left at the bottom of the bowl? Most of them had tiny cracks in their shells. The steam leaked out slowly, the pressure never built up, and they never got their moment.

4.title: Talking in Taps
4.text: Long before phones, people learned to send words down a wire using nothing but clicks. The system is called Morse code, and its whole alphabet is built from just two sounds. A short click is called a dot. A longer one is called a dash. Every letter has its own mix of dots and dashes. The letter E is the most common letter in English. So it gets the shortest code of all, a single dot. Rare letters get longer codes. To send a message, an operator tapped a small metal key. The clicks raced down a telegraph wire to a distant town. Another operator listened and wrote the letters out. The fastest operators could chat at amazing speed. They could even tell who was tapping just by the rhythm. It was like knowing a friend's voice. One code became famous around the world. Three dots, three dashes, three dots spells SOS, the call for help at sea. It was chosen because it is easy to send and hard to mistake. Radios and phones have long since taken over. But some pilots, sailors, and hobby operators still learn the old clicks. An alphabet with just two sounds turned out to be one of the best ideas ever sent down a wire.

4.title: The Flower That Follows the Sun
4.topic: how young sunflowers track the sun
4.text: A field of young sunflowers performs a slow dance every day, and almost nobody sees it happen. At sunrise, all the flower buds face east, toward the light. As the sun crosses the sky, the young plants turn with it, hour by hour. By evening they face west. Then, during the night, they swing all the way back so they are ready to greet the sunrise again. How does a plant with no muscles turn its head? It grows its way around. On a sunny morning, the west side of the young stem grows a little faster, which tips the flower toward the east. Later in the day the east side takes its turn growing, and the flower leans west. The plant is steering itself with growth, a little like a rower pulling harder on one oar. Scientists tested this by tying some young plants in place so they could not turn. Those plants grew smaller leaves and ended up weaker than their dancing neighbors. Following the sun really does help. Grown-up sunflowers stop the dance. They settle down facing east for good. An east-facing flower warms up faster each morning, and warm flowers get the first visits from bees.

5.title: How a Submarine Sinks on Purpose
5.text: A ship made of steel should sink like a stone. Yet a submarine can float on the surface, dive deep, hover in the middle of the sea, and rise again, all on command. Its secret is a set of huge containers called ballast tanks, built between its inner and outer walls. When the tanks are full of air, the submarine weighs less than the water it pushes aside. The ocean holds it up, and it floats. The crew rides high and dry inside. To dive, the crew opens valves at the top of the tanks. Air hisses out, seawater pours in, and the boat grows heavier. Soon it slips beneath the waves. To rise, the crew does the opposite. Machines push stored air back into the tanks with great force, and the air shoves the water out. The submarine grows lighter and climbs toward the light. Fine control matters just as much as sinking and rising. By moving small amounts of water between tanks, the crew can balance the boat so well that it hangs in the sea without moving up or down at all. A submarine never fights the rule that heavy things sink. It simply changes how heavy it is, whenever it chooses.

5.title: Seeing with Sound
5.text: A bat can chase a moth through a pitch-black forest and never hit a branch. Its eyes are not doing that work. Its ears are. As it flies, the bat sends out fast clicks and squeaks, most of them pitched too high for human ears. The sounds race ahead, strike whatever is in the way, and bounce back as echoes. From each echo, the bat's brain builds a picture. A late echo means a faraway object, and an early echo means something close. If the echo is louder in the left ear, the object lies to the left. Even the feel of the echo carries news. A fluttering moth returns a trembling echo that a still leaf never could. As the bat closes in on its target, it clicks faster and faster. It updates its sound picture many times each second, the way a flashlight blinking quickly lights a path better than one slow flash. This skill is called echolocation, which means finding things by echo. Sailors copied the idea to build sonar for their ships. Doctors use a cousin of it to see inside the body. The bat had the technology first, and it still uses nothing but its own voice.

5.title: Raising a Helper
5.topic: how a service dog puppy is raised and trained
5.text: Some dogs grow up to have real jobs, and their training starts while they are still puppies. Volunteer families called puppy raisers take them home for about a year. The raiser's task sounds odd at first, because it is mostly ordinary life. The puppy rides in elevators and hears grocery carts rattle. It waits calmly in long lines and naps under tables in busy places. A working dog must treat noisy rooms as boring. Every strange sound the puppy shrugs off now is one it will ignore later, when its focus matters most. The puppy also learns simple manners. It walks politely on a leash, comes when called, and settles quietly on a mat. After the first year, the young dog moves on to an expert trainer for harder lessons. There it learns special tasks to match a future partner's needs. Some dogs learn to open doors, pick up dropped keys, or lead the way to an exit. Not every dog passes the course. The ones who do not are adopted as beloved family pets. The dogs that pass are matched with a human partner, and the pair practice together for weeks. By the last day, the puppy that once chewed shoelaces has become a calm, skilled helper.

5.title: Why Skyscrapers Sway
5.text: On a windy day, the top of a very tall building may lean a few feet to one side and then glide slowly back. That movement is not a mistake. The builders planned for it. A tower that refused to bend would have to fight the wind with pure strength, and the wind never gets tired. Instead, a skyscraper is built to sway safely, like a tree that gives a little and then returns. The real problem is the people inside. If the swaying grows too lively, stomachs turn and coffee cups slide. So the builders quiet the motion in clever ways. Some towers grow narrower or even twist as they rise. The odd shape breaks up the smooth flow of wind that would otherwise rock the building in a steady rhythm. Other towers hide a surprise near the top floor. A steel ball or concrete block, as heavy as hundreds of cars, hangs there on thick cables like a giant swing. When the tower sways one way, the great weight lags behind and swings the other way. The two motions cancel, and the building calms down. Visitors far below never guess it is there. The tower is not standing perfectly still, and that is exactly why it stands.

5.title: The Secret Life of Bread
5.text: Bread dough goes into the bowl as a dense, heavy lump. Two hours later it has swelled to twice its size, soft and full of air. The baker did not pump it up. Billions of tiny living things did. Yeast is a fungus made of single cells, so small that a spoonful of dry yeast holds billions of them. The cells sleep in their dry granules until warm water wakes them. Stirred into flour, the yeast begins to feed on the flour's sugars. As it feeds, it gives off a gas called carbon dioxide, the same gas that puts the fizz in soda. The gas forms thousands of tiny bubbles all through the dough. Kneading the dough matters, because kneading builds gluten. Gluten is a stretchy web of protein that traps the bubbles instead of letting them escape. The dough puffs up like a sponge made of a thousand tiny balloons. In the hot oven, the bubbles swell one last time, and then the stretchy walls bake firm and set in place. The holes you see in a slice of bread are the empty rooms the gas left behind. Every sandwich is built on the breath of a fungus, which may be the strangest fact in the kitchen.

5.title: A Camera Made of Nothing
5.text: You can build a working camera out of a dark box and a pin. Poke one tiny hole in the front, hang a thin white screen inside, and point the box at something bright. A picture of the scene appears on the screen, in full color and full motion. There is no lens, no glass, and no battery. There is one strange detail. The picture is upside down. The reason comes from a simple rule. Light travels in straight lines. Every point on a tree outside is bouncing light in all directions, but the tiny hole allows only one narrow beam from each point to enter the box. A beam from the top of the tree angles down through the hole and lands near the bottom of the screen. A beam from the bottom angles up and lands near the top. Straight lines crossing through a small opening flip the whole picture. Artists discovered this trick hundreds of years ago with entire dark rooms. On a bright day, a small hole in a window shade would paint the street scene, upside down, on the far wall. People stood inside the camera. Every camera since, including the one in a phone, is a fancier version of that dark room, a box that catches straight lines of light.

5.title: The First Farmers
5.text: Humans invented farming about ten thousand years ago. Leafcutter ants beat us to it by tens of millions of years. A leafcutter colony looks like a parade of tiny gardeners. Each ant marches home holding a piece of green leaf many times its own weight, like a person carrying a mattress with their teeth. Here is the odd part. The ants never eat those leaves. They cannot digest them. The leaves are not food. They are fertilizer. Deep underground, the colony keeps gardens of a special fungus, pale and spongy, growing in room after room. The ants chew the leaves into a soft mulch and spread it over the fungus, which feeds on the mulch and swells. The fungus is what the ants actually eat, and it grows nowhere else on Earth. The ants are real farmers about it, too. They weed out strange molds that invade the garden. They carry in helpful bacteria, growing right on their bodies, that fight harmful germs. When a young queen flies off to start a new colony, she carries a tiny pinch of the family fungus in her mouth, the way settlers once carried seeds. Whole cities under the soil, fed by gardens, run by insects. Farming was never only a human idea.

5.title: The Tower That Grows
5.text: The Eiffel Tower is taller in summer than in winter. That is not a legend. On a hot afternoon the iron tower can stand about six inches taller than it does on a freezing day. The tower is not growing the way a tree grows. It is expanding. Nearly everything gets a little bigger when it heats up. Heat makes the tiny particles inside a material jiggle faster, and as they jiggle, they push each other slightly farther apart. A cold iron beam is a calm crowd standing close together. A hot one is a dancing crowd that needs more room. For small objects the change is too tiny to notice. Stack up thousands of tons of iron, though, and all those tiny stretches add up to inches. Builders cannot stop metal from doing this, so they plan for it instead. Look down the next time you cross a big bridge and you may see a steel strip full of teeth, like two combs pushed together. That is an expansion joint. On hot days the bridge stretches and the teeth slide together. On cold days it shrinks and they pull apart. The gap gives the bridge room to breathe. Metal will always move with the seasons. Good builders just decide where it is allowed to move.

5.title: The Food That Never Spoils
5.text: Explorers have opened sealed pots from ruins thousands of years old. The honey inside was still golden, still sticky, and still good. Almost every other food on Earth spoils in days or weeks. Honey can last for centuries. What makes it so special? Food spoils when tiny living things, like molds and bacteria, move in and multiply. To grow, those invaders need two main things: water and a comfortable home. Honey refuses them both. First, honey is amazingly dry for a liquid. It is mostly sugar, packed so tight that almost no free water is left in it. When a mold lands on honey, the sugar actually pulls water out of the invader, drying it up before it can settle in. Second, honey is slightly acidic, about as tangy inside as orange juice, and most germs cannot stand that. The bees deserve the credit. They fan nectar with their wings for hours to dry it out. They also add special helpers from their own bodies that make the mix even less friendly to germs. One warning: honey in your pantry may turn cloudy and grainy over time. That is not spoiling. The sugar is just forming crystals. Set the jar in warm water, and it turns clear and golden again, good as the day it was sealed.

5.title: The Sound Makers
5.topic: how movie sound effects are made
5.text: The crunch of boots on snow in a winter movie was probably never snow at all. More likely it was a person in a quiet studio. They were squeezing a sack of cornstarch in time with the actor's steps. That person has one of the strangest jobs in film. They are called Foley artists, and their work fills in all the small sounds a movie needs. Microphones on a film set are aimed at voices. Footsteps, rustling coats, jingling keys, and creaking doors often come out too faint or too messy to use. So after filming ends, Foley artists rebuild those sounds from scratch, one at a time. The studio looks like a junk shop. There are bins of gravel, racks of shoes, squeaky chairs, old door handles, and shelves of things that snap, swish, and rattle. Galloping horses have been played by coconut shells since the early days of radio. Artists clap the shells together in a steady beat. Flapping bird wings are often a pair of leather gloves. A folded umbrella opening quickly can stand in for all sorts of whooshes. The artists watch the movie on a screen while they work. They match every step and rustle, take after take, until the timing is perfect. Done well, the trick is invisible. You never notice the sounds were made twice.

6.title: The Gear Trick
6.topic: how bicycle gears trade speed for force
6.text: A cyclist rolling toward a steep hill flicks a lever, the chain hops onto a larger sprocket, and a climb that looked impossible becomes merely slow. Nothing about the rider's legs has changed. What changed is the bargain the bicycle is making with the road. Gears are a trading system, and the things being traded are effort and distance. In a low gear, one full turn of the pedals rolls the bicycle only a short way forward. That sounds like a bad deal until you notice the payoff, which is that each pedal stroke feels light. The rider gives up speed and gets force in return, spinning easily up a slope that would stall the legs in a stronger gear. On a flat road, the trade runs the other way. A high gear moves the bicycle a long way with every turn of the pedals. Now the rider gives up ease and gets speed, pressing harder on the pedals but flying down the road. The mathematics rides on the sprockets themselves. When a small front ring drives a large rear cog, the wheel turns slowly but with great strength. When a large ring drives a small cog, the wheel spins fast and free. No gear ever gives a rider something for nothing. A machine cannot create effort. It can only spend effort more wisely, and that is why the cyclist reaches the top of the hill still pedaling.

6.title: Rivers of Ice
6.text: A glacier does not look like it is going anywhere. It sits in its mountain valley, white and silent, seemingly as fixed as the peaks around it. Yet a glacier is a river. It simply flows so slowly that a whole winter's travel might be measured with a yardstick. It forms high in the cold mountains, where snow piles up faster than summer can melt it. The deep layers press down on the older snow beneath, crushing it into dense blue ice. Under all that weight, something strange happens. The ice stops acting like a brittle solid and begins to creep downhill, bending around curves the way cold honey bends around a spoon. As it creeps, it works on the land. The glacier plucks boulders from the bedrock and drags them along underneath its body. The trapped stones scrape the valley floor like teeth on a file. Rock walls are ground smooth, polished, and scratched with long parallel lines. The results are easy to spot. A mountain stream cuts a narrow notch shaped like the letter V. A glacier bulldozes a broad trough shaped like the letter U, with steep sides and a wide, flat floor. Long after the ice has melted away, that shape remains behind as a signature. Many of the most famous valleys on Earth are exactly this, the empty beds of vanished rivers of ice.

6.title: The Machine That Multiplied Words
6.topic: how the printing press changed access to books
6.text: Six hundred years ago, a book was a treasure, because every copy was somebody's year of work. Each page was written out by hand, letter by letter, with a sharpened quill. One slip of the pen meant scraping the ink away or living with the mistake. Books cost so much that some libraries chained them to the shelves. Then a metalworker had a simple, powerful idea. He made each letter of the alphabet out of metal, as a small stamp. The stamps could be lined up into words, locked into a frame, rolled with ink, and pressed onto paper. Here was the clever part. When the page was done, the same metal letters could be pulled apart and lined up again to print a completely different page. This invention, called movable type, turned copying into a kind of factory work. A shop with one press could turn out more books in a month than a whole room of hand copiers could finish in years. Better still, every copy matched every other copy exactly. The price of books tumbled, and printed pages poured out of workshops across the land. Ideas began to travel faster than any single messenger could carry them. Readers in distant cities could finally study the very same words and argue about what they meant. The press did not make people smarter. It made knowledge harder to lose and easier to share, and that may matter more.

6.title: Eyes in the Dark
6.topic: how human eyes adapt to darkness
6.text: Step from a bright hallway into a dark room and, for a moment, you are almost blind. Stand still, though, and the darkness slowly sorts itself into furniture, doorways, and shapes. Your eyes are not simply getting used to the dark in some vague way. They are switching equipment. The retina, the thin layer at the back of each eye, contains two kinds of cells that sense light. Cone cells handle daylight and color, but they are nearly useless in dim light. Rod cells are the night shift. They are thousands of times more sensitive, though they see the world only in shades of gray. The rods depend on a special light-catching chemical, and bright light bleaches that chemical away almost completely. In darkness, the supply slowly rebuilds. As it grows, the rods can report fainter and fainter glimmers. The rebuilding takes time. That is why full night vision arrives only after half an hour or more in the dark. There is also a curious hole in it. Rods crowd the outer edges of the retina rather than its center. Because of this, a dim star can vanish when you stare straight at it, then reappear when you glance slightly to one side. Astronomers know the trick well. They learn to study the faintest things in the sky by not quite looking at them.

6.title: Gardens Above the Street
6.text: On a summer afternoon, a big city can be several degrees hotter than the countryside around it. The reason is mostly material. Dark rooftops and black pavement soak up sunlight all day, then release the heat slowly through the night, so the city never quite cools off. One answer to this problem is now spreading across skylines. People are planting gardens on roofs. A green roof begins with a waterproof liner and a layer that lets extra water drain away. Above that goes a few inches of lightweight soil. In the soil grow tough, shallow-rooted plants, chosen because they can survive strong wind and long dry spells. The effect on the building below is immediate. Soil and leaves shade the roof surface from the sun. As the plants release moisture into the air, the roof loses heat, the way sweat cools your skin. On a day when a black tar roof is hot enough to fry an egg, the surface under a garden can be dozens of degrees cooler. The rooms beneath it need far less air conditioning. The benefits pile up outdoors, too. A green roof drinks up heavy rain that would otherwise rush into the street drains all at once. Its flowers become filling stations for bees and butterflies crossing the city. A bare roof spends decades doing nothing but shedding rain. A garden gives it a second job.

6.title: How Your Phone Knows Where You Are
6.text: When a map app draws that little blue dot on your screen, it is using signals from space. High above Earth, about thirty GPS satellites circle the planet. Each one repeats the same message over and over. Here is where I am. Here is the exact time I sent this. Your phone does not talk back. It only listens. The trick is in the timing. Radio signals travel very fast, but not instantly. A message from a faraway satellite lands a tiny bit later than one from a nearby satellite. Your phone measures those tiny delays and turns each one into a distance. Each distance draws an invisible bubble around its satellite. The phone must sit somewhere on that bubble's skin. One satellite is not enough, and neither are two. But where the bubbles from four satellites cross, only one point is left. That point is you. The phone repeats the whole calculation every second as you move. None of this would work with sloppy clocks. An error of even a millionth of a second would throw the answer off by hundreds of meters. So each satellite carries an atomic clock, one of the finest timekeepers ever built. The system was built for ships and planes, but its signals are free for everyone. A tool built on split seconds now guides lost drivers, hikers, and pizza runs alike.

6.title: Why Is the Sky Blue?
6.topic: light scattering and the color of the sky
6.text: Sunlight looks white, but it is really every color mixed together, from red through violet. When that mixed light hits Earth's atmosphere, it starts colliding with the tiny particles of gas that make up the sky. Those collisions do not treat every color the same. Light travels in waves, and each color has its own wavelength. Red waves are long and lazy, while blue waves are short and choppy. The particles of air are far better at knocking short waves off course, so blue light gets scattered, bouncing from particle to particle until it comes at you from every part of the sky. Red and yellow light barrels through mostly in a straight line. Look at any patch of daytime sky away from the sun, and the light reaching your eyes is that scattered blue, arriving by a billion crooked paths. Violet waves are even shorter than blue, so why is the sky not violet? There are two reasons: sunlight holds less violet to begin with, and human eyes are much better at seeing blue. Sunset turns the sky red because the low sun's light must plow through far more air to reach you. By the end of that long trip, nearly all the blue has been scattered off to other places. The long red waves are left to finish the trip. The same rule paints both skies. Blue is the color that gets lost along the way, and at sunset, you are seeing everything that made it through.

6.title: The Journey to Your Faucet
6.topic: how city drinking water is cleaned
6.text: The water in your glass may have started this morning in a river, cloudy with mud and crowded with germs. Between the river and your faucet stands a treatment plant, where the water is cleaned in careful stages. The first stage is simple. Screens strain out sticks, leaves, and trash as the water enters the plant. Next comes an elegant trick. Workers stir in a substance that makes tiny specks of dirt turn sticky. The specks bump together and clump into soft, fluffy blobs, which grow heavier and heavier until they sink. The water then rests in wide, calm pools while the blobs settle to the bottom, carrying most of the dirt down with them. The clearer water on top moves on to the filters, sinking slowly through thick beds of sand and crushed charcoal. These beds trap the fine particles that settling missed, and the charcoal also grabs many of the chemicals that give water odd tastes and smells. The water is now clear, but clear is not the same as safe. Germs too small for any filter may remain, so the plant adds a tiny, carefully measured dose of disinfectant to finish them, with a little left over to guard the water on its trip through miles of pipes. All day long, workers pull samples and test them. Clean water is not luck. It is a process, running quietly all the time, a few blocks from your kitchen.

6.title: The Deepest Place
6.topic: the deep ocean trench and life under pressure
6.text: The deepest known place in the ocean is a long, narrow canyon in the Pacific floor. It plunges almost eleven kilometers down. To grasp that depth, imagine dropping the tallest mountain on Earth into it. The peak would vanish with more than two kilometers of water still overhead. The bottom is a hard place to picture. Sunlight gives up long before reaching it. Below a few hundred meters, the sea fades to total, endless dark. The water is barely above freezing. And above every spot on that floor stands a column of water eleven kilometers tall. It squeezes down with about a thousand times the pressure you feel on land. It would seem impossible for anything to live there. Yet life does. Pale creatures like small shrimp swarm over the mud. Ghostly white fish, soft-bodied and slow, cruise the bottom with no trouble at all. The secret is balance. These animals have no air pockets inside them to be squeezed shut. Their bodies are mostly water, pushing out exactly as hard as the sea pushes in. More people have walked on the Moon than have been to the ocean's deepest floor. The few visitors went down for hours in thick metal balls. Their reports agree on one thing. Even in the coldest, darkest, heaviest corner of the planet, something is alive, and it was there first.

6.title: The Missing Quarter Day
6.text: A year, as everyone learns, is 365 days long. Except that it is not. The Earth actually takes about 365 and one quarter days to finish a lap around the sun. That leftover quarter day seems too small to matter, but calendars are unforgiving. If we ignored it, the calendar would fall behind the real seasons by one full day every four years. The drift would be slow and silent. In forty years, the calendar would be ten days off. In a few centuries, the northern half of the world would find itself shivering through a July that felt like early spring, with every holiday sliding out of its season. The fix is the leap year. Every four years, the calendar quietly adds one extra day at the end of February, sweeping up four leftover quarter days at once and pulling the calendar back in line with the sun. The idea is ancient, but there is a wrinkle. The true leftover is slightly less than a quarter day, so adding a day every four years slightly overcorrects. Over centuries, even that tiny error piles up. So the modern calendar adds one more rule. Century years, like 1900, skip their leap day, unless they divide evenly by four hundred. That is why the year 2000 kept its extra day while 1900 went without. A calendar, it turns out, is not a simple list of days. It is a machine for staying lined up with the sky, patched and tuned by centuries of careful counting.
